narrative:
The model estimates an 85% chance that you will leave your job. In practical terms, among employees with a similar profile, about 85 in 100 were predicted to depart, so the promotion was denied because the organization sees you as a high retention risk, not because your qualifications were judged insufficient. Gender, age, and health information were not used.

The strongest signal was your total years of experience: being in the 6–10 year band pushed the prediction toward leaving more than any other factor. The second was that you reported other job opportunities; this is uncommon among employees predicted to stay and strongly increased the leaving signal. Third, your 1–5 years with your current organization also tilted the prediction toward leaving, though less strongly than your overall experience and outside opportunities. Other profile factors matter—no bonus, no medical insurance, no deserved promotion, and no useful training—but the top three above were the main drivers.

Next, the organization should treat this as a retention review before finalizing promotion decisions: discuss concrete career progression, development, pay and benefits, and how to reduce the pull of outside offers. You should clarify what would keep you engaged and ask for a specific plan; if outside opportunities are serious, raise them openly so both sides can decide.
